question: Why did the integrated spent FCC catalyst recovery route still show a net climate-change burden after product-substitution credits?
expect: premise false: after system expansion the net climate-change impact was negative, −2,257.14 kg CO2-eq per t (a net benefit) (abstract)
rendered:
The document titled "Environmental and Preliminary Economic Assessment of Integrated Resource Recovery from Spent Fluid Catalytic Cracking Catalysts" is the most likely to answer this question.

According to the document, the net climate-change impact of the wet-recovery stage was −1,275.04 kg CO2-eq, and the net climate-change impact of the leaching-residue-valorization stage was −982.10 kg CO2-eq. However, the total net climate-change impact of the integrated system was −2,257.14 kg CO2-eq.

Although the integrated system achieved net environmental benefits across all main EF categories, the leaching-residue-valorization stage still showed a positive climate-change impact of 1,940.11 kg CO2-eq. This suggests that the stage-specific environmental burdens of the leaching-residue-valorization stage were not fully offset by the substitution credits associated with the composite phase-change energy-storage material.

The document states that "the complete integrated system achieves net benefits across all main EF categories through the combined substitution credits from APT and the composite phase change material." However, it also notes that "the leaching-residue-valorization stage should not be characterized as environmentally beneficial in every category; rather, the complete integrated system achieves net benefits across all main EF categories through the combined substitution credits from APT and the composite phase change material."

This suggests that the integrated system still shows a net climate-change burden after product-substitution credits because the leaching-residue-valorization stage has a positive climate-change impact that is not fully offset by the substitution credits.
